question: On 1 January 2023, the EU introduced new maximum levels for the following PFASs and their accumulated content in certain foodstuffs: perfluorooctane sulfonic acid (PFOS), perfluorooctanoic acid (PFOA), perfluorononanoic acid (PFNA) and perfluorohexane sulfonic acid (PFHxS)1. There is evidence of a large-scale PFOA soil contamination in the Bavarian district of Altötting.

As a result, an investigation into wild boar meat was carried out in 77 Upper Austrian municipalities. 10 of the 14 wild boars tested there exceeded the limit for lean meat. The recorded levels in drinking water are currently below the limit, although the new EU limit for drinking water has not been introduced yet2,3. 1.

According to the Commission, how safe is it to consume foods that exceed the new maximum levels but are allowed to remain on the market until their ‘best before’ or ‘use-by’ date, provided that they were placed on the market before 1 January?
In addition to introducing maximum levels, will the Commission provide assistance in the event of a large-scale contamination?

How detailed are the technical guidelines regarding the methods of analysis for the monitoring of PFASs, which, according to Article 13(7) of the Drinking Water Directive, must be drawn up by the Commission and are necessary for the introduction of an EU limit?
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (8.3.2024) Boar meat placed on the market after 1 January 2023 needs to comply with the maximum levels (MLs) for perfluoroalkyl substances (PFAS).

Since no such EU levels applied before 1 January 2023, boar meat placed on the market before that date and containing PFAS at levels above the ML can remain on the market, unless Member States would conclude in accordance with Article 14(1) of Regulation (EU) No 178/20021 on the basis of a risk assessment considering consumption patterns and actual levels of PFAS that such meat is not safe.

In that case the meat is not considered to have been lawfully placed on the market and Member States can take appropriate enforcement actions. Support for the decontamination of soils and water by the Commission is only possible if the polluter-pays principle has been observed. Public bodies may only support decontamination where the polluter is not known or cannot ensure the decontamination.

In the case of Altötting, the contamination stems from a chemical company which shall ensure decontamination. Even when the polluter-pays principle is observed, decontamination can only be supported by the European Regional Development Fund (ERDF) if the region concerned has programmed such support. This is not the case of the 2021-27 Bayern ERDF programme.

In accordance with Article 13(7) of the recast Drinking Water Directive2, the Commission is preparing the technical guidelines regarding methods for monitoring ‘Sum of PFAS’ and ‘PFAS Total’ in water intended for human consumption.

Following the establishment of these technical guidelines, Member States may then decide to use either one or both of the parameters ‘PFAS Total’ or ‘Sum of PFAS’, to be complied with by January 2026.
1 Regulation (EU) No 178/2002 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 28 January 2002 laying down

the general principles and requirements of food law, establishing the European Food Safety Authority and laying down procedures in matters of food safety (OJ L 031 1.2.2002, p. 1). 2 Directive (EU) 2020/2184 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 16 December 2020 on the quality of water intended for human consumption (OJ L 435 23.12.2020, p. 1-62).
